content: Continuing education refers to a broad range of post-secondary learning activities and programs. These include degree-credit courses taken by non-traditional students, non-degree career training, workforce training, formal personal enrichment courses (offered both on-campus and online), self-directed learning (such as through internet interest groups, clubs, or personal research activities), and experiential learning applied to problem-solving. General continuing education is similar to adult education in that it is designed for adult learners, particularly those beyond the typical undergraduate college or university age. However, it generally does not include basic instruction such as literacy, English language skills, or programs like vocational training or GED preparation. Instead, as the term implies, it assumes that the student already has an educational foundation and is continuing to build upon it. In the United States, continuing education often involves enrollment in college or university credit-granting courses, typically by part-time students, and is frequently offered through a division or school of continuing education, sometimes referred to as a university extension or extension school. It can also involve non-credit-granting courses, often taken for personal enrichment rather than vocational purposes, though some non-credit courses may also serve vocational functions. Many of these non-credit courses are offered by community colleges. The University of Wisconsin-Madison was the first academic institution in the U.S. to offer a recognizable continuing education program in 1904. In 1969, Empire State College, part of the State University of New York, became the first institution in the U.S. to focus exclusively on providing higher education to adult learners. Within the realm of continuing education, professional continuing education is a specific type of learning activity that typically involves the issuance of a certificate or Continuing Education Units (CEUs) to document attendance at a designated seminar or instructional course. Licensing bodies in various fields often require professionals to engage in continuing education to maintain their licenses. These requirements are intended to encourage professionals to expand their knowledge base and stay current with new developments in their field. Depending on the profession, these requirements may be fulfilled through college or university coursework, extension courses, or attendance at conferences and seminars. Ten contact hours of instruction are equivalent to one Continuing Education Unit. The delivery methods for continuing education can include traditional classroom lectures and laboratory sessions. However, a significant portion of continuing education relies on distance learning, which may involve independent study, videotaped or CD-ROM materials, broadcast programming, online or internet-based delivery, and interactive online courses. In addition to independent study, conference-style group study, which may include study networks (often meeting online) and various types of seminars or workshops, can also be utilized to facilitate learning. A combination of traditional, distance, and conference-style study—or any two of these three methods—may be employed for a particular continuing education course or program.
